title: Generalized LIMDDs: Succinctness and Canonicity for Decision Diagrams Modulo a Group
authors: Arend-Jan Quist, Alexis de Colnet, Thomas Reps, Alfons Laarman
abstract: A reduced ordered decision diagram is the minimal automaton of a function on words of fixed length: its nodes are the residuals, and reduction is the Myhill--Nerode quotient. We study what happens when that quotient is coarsened by a group. Fix a group $G$ acting on residuals, merge two nodes when their residuals lie in one $G$-orbit, and record the group element on the edge. For functions $\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb{C}$ and $G$ the Pauli group this is the Local Invertible Map Decision Diagram. We take $G$ from the two-parameter family generated by $C^{\leq k}R_q$, the phase rotation of order $q$ with up to $k$ control qubits, with and without the bit flip $X$. We show that this gives exponential succinctness improvements compared to Pauli-LIMDD, and we determine the succinctness order of the family completely. The separating objects are hypergraph states, which can always be efficiently represented by some member of the family. We settle the tractability of five queries and eight transformations, which is invariant across the family, and shows the same behavior as Pauli-LIMDD. We give a five-rule reduction system whose normal forms are unique for every member of the family, and we show that this canonical form is computable in polynomial time in the size of the LIMDD. We show that, when coarsening beyond the (anti-)diagonal groups, the calculation of a minimal sized normal form turns out to be non-local and it might to rebuild the whole diagram.
summary: This paper generalizes decision diagrams by quotienting the state space by a group action derived from quantum gates (like phase rotations and bit flips). It proves that this generalization yields exponentially more succinct representations for quantum states, specifically characterizing hypergraph states. The methodology combines group theory with advanced algebraic minimization techniques to establish unique, efficiently computable canonical forms.
main_problem: The paper studies the structure, succinctness, and canonicity of decision diagrams when the standard equality condition is replaced by a quotienting by a group action (Generalized LIMDDs).
main_result: The proposed family of groups allows for unique normal forms computable in polynomial time, and the diagrams precisely characterize hypergraph states.
method: The authors use algebraic methods involving group theory (quotienting by group orbits) and linear algebra (Gaussian elimination over Z2 and Zq) to establish canonical forms and determine the succinctness order.
model_or_system: The model involves representing quantum states (specifically hypergraph states) using L-labeled decision diagrams whose edge labels are drawn from a group $\langle G angle$ generated by phase rotations ($R_q$) and controlled by qubits ($C_{\le k}R_q$).
key_observables: Succinctness (diagram size), canonicity (existence of unique normal form), and the structure of the stabilizer subgroup $	ext{Stab}(v)$.
important_parameters: The control arity ($k$) and the root order ($q$) of the generating group $\langle G angle$ are key parameters determining the exponential hierarchy of succinctness.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the structure of the group $\langle G angle$ and relies on establishing canonical representations for nodes satisfying specific reduction rules (R1-R5).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates an example of a $\langle R_3, X angle$-LIMDD and its 0-edge normal form. Figure 2 provides a 'Succinctness map' showing the exponential separations between different LIMDD families based on $q$, $k$, and $X$.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first defining the generalized diagrams, then characterizing the group structure $\langle G angle$, establishing the minimization procedure for the normal form using linear algebra, and finally proving the exponential succinctness gains and the characterization of hypergraph states.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, mathematically rigorous framework for compressing the description of complex quantum states (like those arising in quantum computation) using algebraic structures derived from quantum gates.
